Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes): Acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze, shortness of breath, and cough for 2–3 days; known asthma; atopy (eczema, hay fever/allergic rhinitis). Family history: brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes): Brother asthmatic; sister with eczema.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation likely on a background of atopy/allergic airway inflammation.
- Key findings supporting working diagnosis: Known asthma; wheeze and shortness of breath with exertion and at rest; coughing; partial response to blue inhaler; daily use of inhaled corticosteroid (brown inhaler) planned to increase; baseline peak flow 380 (previously normal for this patient); no fever or purulent sputum; patient able to perform peak flow assessment planned; family history of asthma and eczema.
- Relevant differentials from DDx that support or refine impression:
  - Acute asthma exacerbation (High): Consistent with asthma history, current wheeze, SOB, poor response to SABA, and plan to escalate controller therapy.
  - Viral/URTI-triggered bronchospasm with asthma (Medium): Onset over several days with cough and dyspnea; atopy increases susceptibility to virus-driven bronchospasm.
  - Allergic/Atopy-driven asthma (Medium): Atopic background (hay fever, eczema) and family history support chronic allergic airway inflammation contributing to symptoms.
  - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction with underlying atopy/asthma (Medium): Symptoms initiated with running; exertional dyspnea; ongoing symptoms with daily controller use.
  - Other considerations (Low likelihood/unclear at present): Anemia or other metabolic causes not supported by current data.
- Plan details:
  - Acute management: Continue and adjust bronchodilator use; SABA (Salbutamol) to be used as needed, with guidance to avoid excessive reliance (up to every 2 hours during symptoms; if needed more often, this indicates uncontrolled symptoms).
  - Controller therapy: Increase brown inhaler (beclomethasone/Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily.
  - Monitoring: Chest examination and peak flow measurement to be performed; reassess response to escalation.
  - Red flags and escalation: If breathing worsens or patient deteriorates, go to A&E.
  - Follow-up: Schedule GP review in the next few days; in interim, continue current plan and monitor symptoms.
  - Additional interventions: If clinically indicated after assessment, antibiotics and systemic steroids may be considered; currently not started.

- Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Known asthma with current wheeze, shortness of breath, cough; inadequate relief from SABA; plan to escalate controller therapy and monitor peak flow; no ED red flags yet.
- Viral/URTI-triggered bronchospasm with asthma
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Onset over 2–3 days with cough and dyspnea; atopy increases susceptibility to virus-driven bronchospasm.
- Allergic/Atopy-driven asthma
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Atopic history (hay fever, eczema) and family history of asthma support chronic allergic airway inflammation contributing to symptoms.
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (with underlying atopy/asthma)
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Symptoms began with running; exertional dyspnea/wheeze; daily controller use with ongoing symptoms.
- Anemia or other metabolic causes (less likely)

  - Justification: Exertional dyspnea could reflect anemia, but no supporting data (fatigue, pallor, labs).
